clue.text: Wicked display by Satan, never ending

indicators.note: something that never ends is cut off before its final letter

blocks.note: a demo is a demonstration or display
Old Nick is a nickname for the Devil

explanation.surface: Satan puts on a show of pure wickedness that goes on forever.
explanation.walkthrough: DEMONIC is DEMO plus NIC(K); Old Nick is a traditional name for the Devil. 'Satan' tempts you towards DEMON, but the Devil gives only the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: Demonic describes something devilish or evil, a close synonym of wicked.

clue.text: Unearth bulbs at headquarters?

blocks.note: whimsical sense: to ... plants, taking them out of their pots
a military ... is a regiment's headquarters

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is a coinage: DE- (remove from) plus POT, read as taking bulbs out of their pots. The question mark flags the invention.
explanation.definitionFit: A depot is the base or headquarters of a regiment, where its stores and recruits are kept.

clue.text: Cockney couple taking a stroll

indicators.note: a Cockney accent drops the H, so the words are rendered as a Londoner would say them

blocks.note: a couple is 'me and her', said with the D softened and the H dropped

explanation.surface: A pair of East Londoners go out for a walk together.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class London dialect, famous for dropping the H, so 'me and her' becomes 'me an' 'er'.
explanation.definitionFit: A meander is a leisurely, wandering walk, so it can stand for a stroll.

clue.text: Pin down part of the body

blocks.note: first meaning: to fix or identify exactly
second meaning: the horny plate on a finger or toe

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one instruction about locating a body part; it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To nail something is to pin it down precisely, and a nail also grows on every finger and toe.

clue.text: Would changed bat put off cricketer's dismissal?

indicators.note: put off read as disturbed or thrown out of order, so the words before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the fifteen letters of these three words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A batsman wonders whether swapping his bat would have spared him being given out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the letters to shuffle; 'put off' does the work. In cricket the batsman is out when the bowler catches his own delivery.
explanation.definitionFit: Caught and bowled is a way a batsman is dismissed in cricket, when the bowler takes the catch.

clue.text: Reasonable space found in Mensa for classicists

indicators.note: something found in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: mensa is the Latin word for table, as classicists know
an en is a printer's space

explanation.surface: A sensible amount of room was set aside at the Mensa society for scholars of the classics.
explanation.walkthrough: Mensa looks like the high-IQ society, but 'for classicists' tells you to read it as a Latin word; an en is a printer's unit of spacing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenable position is one that can be defended or maintained, so it is reasonable.

clue.text: Just what it took for old hams to get a good reception?

definitions.text: Just what it took for old hams to get a good reception?

blocks.note: surface reading: exactly the thing that was needed, something excellent

blocks.clueFragment: for old hams to get a good reception?
blocks.note: setter's reading: old crystal radio sets used a fine wire contact to pick up signals, which amateur radio operators relied on

explanation.surface: Washed-up actors finally win a warm welcome thanks to something perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: Hams are amateur radio enthusiasts, not bad actors; early crystal sets used a thin wire probe nicknamed after a pet's facial hair to tune in.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for something excellent, and literally names the wire contact in early radio receivers.

clue.text: Ballet enthusiast takes the biscuit

blocks.note: a nut is a fanatic, as in a fitness nut
a cracker is a thin crisp biscuit

explanation.surface: A dance fan outdoes everyone else in silliness, as in 'that takes the biscuit'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is a British idiom for being the most outrageous; here it is split, with 'takes' only joining the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nutcracker is Tchaikovsky's Christmas ballet, so it names one particular ballet.

clue.text: Club employee finds cat in empty bar

indicators.note: an empty word has had its contents removed, leaving only its outside letters
one thing in another sits inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: the word bar with its middle letter gone
the ounce is the snow leopard, a big cat

explanation.surface: A nightclub worker discovers a cat in a bar with no customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a cat that crosswords love. It sits inside B...R.
explanation.definitionFit: A bouncer is the doorman employed by a nightclub to keep out troublemakers.

clue.text: Without sound daughter expired

blocks.note: ex is Latin for out of or without, as in ex dividend
hale means healthy, sound in body
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A daughter died silently, with no noise at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without sound' reads as silently, but 'sound' means healthy and 'expired' means breathed out rather than died.
explanation.definitionFit: To expire is literally to breathe out, which is what exhaled means.

clue.text: Pharmacist's leader gets licence for bromide

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of pharmacist
latitude is freedom or licence to act

explanation.surface: A chemist's boss is allowed to dispense a sedative.
explanation.walkthrough: Bromide was once a pharmacy sedative, which suits the surface, but here it means a dull, trite remark.
explanation.definitionFit: A bromide is a tired, unoriginal remark meant to soothe, the same as a platitude.

clue.text: Stir the emotions, but only a little

blocks.note: first meaning: to move someone emotionally
second meaning: a small amount, as in a pinch of salt

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as advice to move people only gently; it is two separate meanings joined.
explanation.definitionFit: To touch someone is to move them emotionally, and a touch is a slight amount of something.

clue.text: Stew in need of attention

blocks.note: first meaning: a fuss or state of agitation
second meaning: still waiting to be done, as on a list of tasks

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stew' looks like food, but it means being in a flap, as in 'getting in a stew'.
explanation.definitionFit: A to-do is a commotion or fuss, and a job still to do awaits attention.

clue.text: First glimpse of tent upset Charlie at camp

indicators.note: the first glimpse of a thing is its very beginning, so only the opening letter is used
upset means knocked over or disordered, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the opening letter of tent
these letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Charlie was dismayed the moment he saw the tent at the campsite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'camp' looks like a campsite, matching the tent, but it is the adjective meaning exaggerated and showy; 'at' is part of the anagram letters as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Camp behaviour is deliberately exaggerated and showy, which is what theatrical describes.

clue.text: Unruly little boy stands on army messenger

indicators.note: in a down clue, a word that stands is set upright, so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: Sid is a short form of the boy's name Sidney
an orderly is a soldier who carries messages for an officer

explanation.surface: A naughty small boy climbs on top of a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the reversed name sits before the messenger.
explanation.definitionFit: Disorderly means out of control and badly behaved, just like unruly.

clue.text: Ignoring me, tortured American finds treatment for bruises

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out, so those letters are removed
something tortured is twisted out of shape, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then removed

explanation.surface: A battered American, paying no attention to the speaker, discovers a cure for his bruises.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ME out of AMERICAN to leave A,R,I,C,A,N, then rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Arnica is a herbal ointment made from a mountain plant, used to soothe bruises.

clue.text: Scoundrel housed by offspring is rendered safe

indicators.note: something housed by another lives inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

blocks.note: seed means descendants, as in biblical usage
a cur is a contemptible man

explanation.surface: A rogue taken in by his own children is now out of danger.
explanation.definitionFit: Something secured has been made safe and protected, for example locked or fastened.

clue.text: Bloody deal, perhaps, for giant Californian

blocks.note: red is the colour of blood
deal is pine or fir timber, an example of wood

explanation.surface: A violent business agreement is struck on behalf of a big man from California.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deal' is a timber, not an agreement; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of a kind of wood.
explanation.definitionFit: The coast redwood of California is the tallest tree in the world, a true giant.

clue.text: Upper class thief offers chance of goods for small outlay

definitions.text: offers chance of goods for small outlay

blocks.note: first meaning: A. J. ..., the gentleman burglar of E. W. Hornung's stories

blocks.clueFragment: offers chance of goods for small outlay
blocks.note: second meaning: runs a lottery in which cheap tickets may win prizes

explanation.walkthrough: Raffles is the cricketing gentleman thief of Edwardian fiction; the second half is the verb for running a prize draw.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffles is a fictional posh burglar, and to raffle is to sell tickets that could win a prize.

clue.text: Queen supports formal attire for lady's maid

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing supporting another sits beneath it, so it is placed second

blocks.note: evening dress is formal wear
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher

explanation.surface: The monarch backs a formal dress code for her female servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser is a servant who helps someone put on clothes, the duty of a lady's maid.

clue.text: Carnivores showing inward desire for laughs?

indicators.note: inward means directed inside, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: ha is a laugh, so two or more are has
a yen is a longing

explanation.surface: Meat-eaters reveal a secret wish to be amused, and of course these animals famously laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'laughing hyena' is named for its cackling call, which gives the clue its joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyenas are meat-eating African mammals, so they are carnivores.

clue.text: Stimulant provided by eating out around noon

indicators.note: out here means wrong or disordered, so the preceding letters are shuffled
going around something encloses it, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
N is short for noon

explanation.surface: A pick-me-up comes from dining out at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: The shuffled letters of EATING wrap around N, which falls after the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An antigen is a substance that stimulates the immune system to produce antibodies.

clue.text: Animal filmed wandering beside river

indicators.note: wandering means moving about aimlessly, so the letters before it are rearranged
beside means next to, so the two parts are set side by side

blocks.note: taken as written
the Ouse is a river in England

explanation.surface: A creature was caught on camera roaming along a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ouse is the name of several English rivers, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: A field mouse is a small wild rodent, one specific kind of animal.

clue.text: Stage favourites making a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the word is read going back the other way

blocks.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: Popular performers return to the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests theatre, but it means a phase or step in a process.
explanation.definitionFit: A step is one stage in a process, as in going step by step.

clue.text: King has dirty coat — substitute needed

indicators.note: a coat covers the outside of something, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: poxy is British slang for worthless or grotty, literally diseased
R is Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A monarch's coat is filthy, so a stand-in has to be found.
explanation.walkthrough: Poxy is a British slang word meaning shabby or rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: A proxy is someone authorised to act in another's place, a substitute.

clue.text: Advantage held by favoured generation

indicators.note: held by means contained within, so the letters sit inside the following words

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A privileged generation keeps its head start over others.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the edge over a rival means holding a slight advantage.

clue.text: Slacker dropping out first — he's sure to fail

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the word before is used
dropping something lets it fall away, so it is removed

blocks.note: looser means more slack
the opening letter of out

explanation.surface: A lazy person who quits early is bound to come to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slacker' reads as an idler, but it is the comparative of slack; one O is taken out of LOOSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is someone who always fails, so he's sure to fail describes him.

clue.text: After break-up, Google's ID remains hidden

indicators.note: after something is broken up its parts are scattered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: these letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Once a company is split up, the search giant's identity stays secret.
explanation.walkthrough: To lie doggo is an informal British phrase for keeping quiet and out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: To lie doggo is an idiom meaning to stay still and concealed, avoiding notice.

clue.text: Stopped crossing river and went wrong

indicators.note: crossing something means straddling it, so one piece spans the other

blocks.note: stayed means stopped or halted
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Someone halted while fording a river and then lost the way.
explanation.definitionFit: To stray is to wander from the right path, morally or literally going wrong.

clue.text: Informal police squad is very small, so they say

indicators.note: what people say is spoken, so the words are taken by their sound

blocks.note: is shortened to 's, and weeny means tiny

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a casual group of officers is tiny.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sweeney is London slang for the Flying Squad, from rhyming slang Sweeney Todd; a 1970s TV drama used the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sweeney is a slang name for the Metropolitan Police's Flying Squad, a crime-fighting unit.
